questions.q: What does SAST analyze, and how?
options: Running application traffic, captured by a network proxy
Source code, examined for vulnerability patterns without being executed
Container images, scanned layer by layer after they are built
User behavior logs collected from production
questions.explain: SAST stands for Static Application Security Testing — it examines source code for known vulnerability patterns without ever running the program.

questions.q: What does taint analysis specifically trace?
options: Whether a container image was built from an approved base image
Whether data from an untrusted source can reach a dangerous function without validation
Whether a dependency has a known CVE
Whether a secret was committed to git history
questions.explain: Taint analysis follows the path untrusted data takes through a program, flagging cases where it reaches a sensitive operation (like a database call) without being validated.

questions.q: At Northbridge Retail, where did developers see the code scanning alert for the checkout service's inventory lookup?
options: Only in a weekly email digest
In the repository's Security tab and as a results check directly on the pull request
In a separate ticketing system unrelated to GitHub
Nowhere — alerts are silent until someone manually runs a report
questions.explain: GitHub code scanning surfaces findings in both the Security tab and as a check result on the pull request itself, so developers don't need to leave their workflow.

questions.q: Why does a SAST finding require developer triage rather than automatic action?
options: Because SAST tools are always correct and triage is just a formality
Because pattern-based analysis can produce false positives that aren't actually exploitable
Because SAST findings expire automatically after 24 hours
Because triage is required by law in every country
questions.explain: Pattern matching can flag code that resembles a vulnerability but isn't exploitable in context, so a human needs to confirm, fix, or document a dismissal.

questions.q: Which of these would SAST NOT catch on its own?
options: A SQL query built by concatenating unvalidated user input
A known critical CVE in an imported open-source library
A regular expression vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking
A cryptographic function known to be weak, written directly in the code
questions.explain: SAST analyzes the code you wrote, not the vulnerabilities inside imported dependencies — that gap is covered by dependency and composition scanning in Lesson 16.
